content: The document titled Understanding barriers to quality of care: An approach for conducting a situational analysis of water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) and quality in health care facilities provides a detailed framework for assessing and addressing gaps in WASH services within health care settings. This publication outlines a structured methodology for conducting a national situational analysis of water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) services in health care facilities. The analysis serves as a foundation for improving the quality of care provided in these facilities. It emphasizes the importance of WASH services in supporting core aspects of quality, equity, and dignity in health care delivery, particularly in maternity and primary care settings where such services are often lacking. Globally, one in four health care facilities lacks basic water services, one in ten has no sanitation services, and one in three lacks hand hygiene facilities at the point of care or systems for waste segregation. These gaps are even more pronounced in Least Developed Countries, where twice as many facilities lack basic WASH services. The absence of these services undermines the ability to provide quality care, compromises patient safety, and violates fundamental human rights. The document highlights that WASH services are essential for effective infection prevention and control (IPC), patient safety, and the delivery of care in a clean, dignified, and respectful environment. These services are also critical for achieving universal health coverage (UHC) and primary health care commitments, as outlined in the UHC High-Level Declaration and the Astana Declaration. The situational analysis process described in the document includes preparatory stages, data collection, analysis, and dissemination of results. It identifies barriers to quality care, explores potential solutions, and provides evidence-based recommendations for policy revision and resource allocation. The approach is designed to help national governments, UN organizations, and partners understand policy gaps, raise awareness of problems, tailor interventions, and advocate for additional financing. The methodology is based on experiences from previous analyses conducted in countries such as Cambodia, Ethiopia, Ghana, Hungary, Rwanda, Serbia, and Tajikistan. It was further refined during the 2019 Global Meeting on WASH in health care facilities held in Livingstone, Zambia. The document also underscores the importance of embedding WASH indicators into existing health monitoring systems to obtain nationally representative data in a systematic and sustainable manner. Where resources are limited, targeted sub-national assessments in specific regions or districts can provide valuable insights and generate political will for action. The publication concludes by emphasizing the need for countries to develop costed roadmaps and national policies to strengthen and sustain WASH services in health care facilities. It also calls for systematic situational analyses to address data gaps and inform evidence-based decision-making. This professional summary captures the essence of the document while maintaining a clear and detailed explanation of its content.
